NAME AVAILABILITY AND RESERVATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Meridian Ventures, Inc. · stock corporation

NAME AVAILABILITY AND RESERVATION INFORMATION SHEET — PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This information sheet addresses California's requirement that a proposed corporate or limited liability company name be distinguishable on the records of the California Secretary of State before an entity can be formed under that name, and the procedure by which a proposed name can be reserved with the Secretary of State in advance of filing formation documents. It relates to the proposed name "Meridian Ventures, Inc." under consideration for a stock corporation to be formed in California. This document is not this project's LLC Articles of Organization or Articles of Incorporation document — those documents state the name that is ultimately included in the formation filing itself. This document instead addresses a distinct, often earlier step: whether a proposed name is legally available for use, what categories of words in a proposed name can require separate regulatory approval, how a proposed name can be reserved for a period of time before the formation documents are filed, and what happens if an entity is nonetheless formed under a name that turns out not to have been distinguishable. This information sheet is educational only. It does not itself reserve "Meridian Ventures, Inc.," or any other name, with the California Secretary of State, and it does not determine whether "Meridian Ventures, Inc." is in fact distinguishable from any name already on file or under reservation.

THE DISTINGUISHABLE-NAME STANDARD
California law imposes the same two-part naming standard on both corporations and limited liability companies, stated in parallel language in two separate statutes. For a corporation, the name "shall not be a name that the Secretary of State determines is likely to mislead the public" and must be "distinguishable in the records of the Secretary of State" from the names of other corporations, from foreign corporations authorized to transact business in California, and from names currently under reservation. The California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act imposes the identical two-part standard on an LLC's name — not likely to mislead the public, and distinguishable in the Secretary of State's records from other LLC names, from foreign LLCs authorized to transact intrastate business here, and from names currently reserved under the LLC reservation statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The name of a corporation shall not be a name that the Secretary of State determines is likely to mislead the public and shall be distinguishable in the records of the Secretary of State from all of the following: (1) The name of any corporation. (2) The name of any foreign corporation authorized to transact intrastate business in this state."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 201(b), California General Corporation Law, the distinguishable-name standard for corporations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=201.)
  "The name of a limited liability company shall not be a name that the Secretary of State determines is likely to mislead the public and shall be distinguishable in the records of the Secretary of State from all of the following: (1) The name of any limited liability company. (2) The name of any foreign limited liability company authorized to transact intrastate business in this state."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.08(b), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, the distinguishable-name standard for LLCs (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.08.)
  Known gap: Cal. Corp. Code § 201 (corporations) and Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.08 (limited liability companies) are separate, independently enacted statutory sections in different titles of the Corporations Code — not subsections of a single section — so the two citations below are independent sources corroborating a parallel rule, not two views of one provision. This document's research covered only corporations and limited liability companies; it did not research the naming rules that apply to general partnerships, limited partnerships, limited liability partnerships, or nonprofit corporations, which may differ. Neither statute quoted here states the specific comparison methodology the Secretary of State uses to decide whether two names are "distinguishable" (for example, how differences in punctuation, spacing, capitalization, or required entity designators like "LLC" or "Inc." are treated) — that operational detail, to the extent it exists, is Secretary of State administrative practice rather than statutory text, and this document does not state it because it was not verified against a primary legal source.

NAME RESERVATION PROCEDURE AND DURATION
California law lets a person apply to the Secretary of State, and pay the prescribed fee, to reserve the exclusive use of a proposed corporate or LLC name before filing formation documents. For a corporation, upon payment of the fee, an applicant "may... obtain from the Secretary of State a certificate of reservation of any name not prohibited by subdivision (b) [the distinguishable-name standard], and upon the issuance of the certificate the name stated therein shall be reserved for a period of 60 days." For a limited liability company, if the Secretary of State finds that the applied-for name is available, the statute directs that "it shall reserve the name for the applicant's exclusive use for up to 60 days and issue a certificate of reservation." Neither statute permits back-to-back reservations of the same name: the Secretary of State will not issue certificates reserving the same name for two or more consecutive 60-day periods to the same applicant or for the same person's benefit, nor consecutive reservations of a name so similar to another name that it would fail the distinguishable-name standard. For an LLC name reservation specifically, the statute also allows the reservation's owner to transfer it to another person by delivering a signed notice of the transfer to the Secretary of State.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Any applicant may, upon payment of the fee prescribed therefor in Article 3 (commencing with Section 12180) of Chapter 3 of Part 2 of Division 3 of Title 2 of the Government Code, obtain from the Secretary of State a certificate of reservation of any name not prohibited by subdivision (b), and upon the issuance of the certificate the name stated therein shall be reserved for a period of 60 days."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 201(e), California General Corporation Law, corporate name reservation procedure and 60-day duration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=201.)
  "a person may apply to reserve the exclusive use of the name of a limited liability company or foreign limited liability company, including an alternative name for a foreign limited liability company whose name is not available. If the Secretary of State finds that the name applied for is available, it shall reserve the name for the applicant’s exclusive use for up to 60 days and issue a certificate of reservation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.09(a), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, LLC name reservation procedure and 60-day duration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.09.)
  Known gap: Cal. Corp. Code § 201(e) (corporations) and Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.09 (limited liability companies) are separate, independently enacted sections and are treated as independent sources here. Both statutes reference a filing fee set elsewhere, in Government Code Article 3 (commencing with Section 12180) of Chapter 3, Part 2, Division 3, Title 2 — this document's research did not extend to that separate Government Code fee schedule, so no specific dollar amount is stated; the current fee is published by the Secretary of State. This document verified the reservation-transfer provision only for LLC name reservations (§ 17701.09(b)); the corporation naming statute (§ 201) as verified here does not contain a comparable transfer provision, and this document does not state that corporations can or cannot transfer a name reservation because that was not independently verified.

RESTRICTED WORDS REQUIRING SEPARATE REGULATORY APPROVAL
Beyond the general distinguishable-name standard, California law separately restricts specific categories of words in a corporation's or LLC's name. For a corporation, the Secretary of State "shall not file articles setting forth a name in which 'bank,' 'trust,' 'trustee,' or related words appear, unless the certificate of approval of the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation is attached" to the articles — meaning those words are not banned outright for a corporation, but are conditioned on a named regulator's prior approval. A separate corporate-naming statute imposes the same kind of approval condition where the corporation's business is to be an insurer: the Secretary of State "shall not file articles in which the business is to be an insurer unless the certificate of the Insurance Commissioner approving the corporate name is attached." The LLC-naming statute takes a different approach to some of the same words: rather than an approval pathway, it flatly bars an LLC's name from including "'bank,' 'trust,' 'trustee,' 'incorporated,' 'inc.,' 'corporation,' or 'corp.'" and from including "'insurer' or 'insurance company' or any other words suggesting that it is in the business of issuing policies of insurance and assuming insurance risks" — there is no statutory mechanism, as verified here, for an LLC to obtain approval to use those words the way a corporation can for the banking- and insurance-related terms.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The Secretary of State shall not file articles setting forth a name in which “bank,” “ trust,” “trustee,” or related words appear, unless the certificate of approval of the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation is attached thereto."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 201(a), California General Corporation Law, bank/trust/trustee name approval requirement for corporations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=201.)
  "The Secretary of State shall not file articles in which the business is to be an insurer unless the certificate of the Insurance Commissioner approving the corporate name is attached thereto."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 201.5, California General Corporation Law, insurer-name approval requirement for corporations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=201.5.)
  "The name shall not include the words “bank,” “trust,” “trustee,” “incorporated,” “inc.,” “corporation,” or “corp.” and shall not include the words “insurer” or “insurance company” or any other words suggesting that it is in the business of issuing policies of insurance and assuming insurance risks."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.08(e), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, outright bank/trust/insurer word restriction for LLCs (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.08.)
  Known gap: Cal. Corp. Code § 201(a), § 201.5, and § 17701.08(e) are three separate, independently enacted statutory provisions (§ 201.5 was added by a different, later-dated bill than § 201, and § 17701.08 sits in an entirely different title of the code governing LLCs rather than corporations), so the citations below are independent sources, not subsections of one section presented as several. This document verified only the banking/trust/trustee and insurer-related restricted-word rules. It did not find, and does not claim to have verified, any statutory restriction in the Corporations Code tying other words — such as words suggesting affiliation with a specific licensed profession (e.g., "attorney," "CPA," "engineer") — to a name-approval requirement; if such rules exist, they were not located during this research and are not addressed here. This document also does not state the current fee or application procedure for obtaining the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation's or the Insurance Commissioner's approval, since that operational detail was not verified.

CONSEQUENCE OF FILING UNDER A NAME THAT IS NOT ACTUALLY DISTINGUISHABLE
California's naming statutes do not provide that a corporation's or LLC's existence is automatically dissolved, or that its articles are automatically void, if the entity's name turns out not to have been distinguishable at the time of filing. Instead, both statutes provide a narrower, forward-looking remedy: for a corporation, "the use... of a name in violation of this section may be enjoined notwithstanding the filing of its articles by the Secretary of State," and the identical rule applies to an LLC — "the use by a limited liability company of a name in violation of this section may be enjoined notwithstanding the filing of its articles by the Secretary of State." In other words, the statutory consequence for continuing to use a name that violates the distinguishable-name standard is that a court may enjoin (order a stop to) that use, even though the Secretary of State already accepted the filing — the filing itself is not automatically undone.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The use by a corporation of a name in violation of this section may be enjoined notwithstanding the filing of its articles by the Secretary of State."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 201(d), California General Corporation Law, injunction remedy for a noncompliant corporate name (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=201.)
  "The use by a limited liability company of a name in violation of this section may be enjoined notwithstanding the filing of its articles by the Secretary of State."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.08(c), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, injunction remedy for a noncompliant LLC name (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.08.)
  Known gap: Cal. Corp. Code § 201(d) (corporations) and Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.08(c) (limited liability companies) are separate, independently enacted sections and are treated as independent sources here. Neither statute, as verified, states who may bring an action to enjoin the use of a noncompliant name, what showing is required, or any other procedural detail of that remedy — this document does not state those details because they were not verified against primary text. This document also did not verify, and does not describe, any Secretary of State administrative practice of screening or rejecting a proposed name for distinguishability at the time of filing (as opposed to at the time of a separate name-reservation request) — to the extent such an intake screening practice exists, it is an administrative practice rather than something stated in the statutory text quoted above, and it is disclosed here as an honest gap rather than assumed.

CLOSING AND NAME RESERVATION REQUEST RECORD
Name availability and reservation information sheet relating to the proposed stock corporation name "Meridian Ventures, Inc.," prepared by Acme, Inc.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Acme, Inc.: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes California's statutory distinguishable-name standard for corporations and limited liability companies, the procedure and duration for reserving a proposed name with the Secretary of State, restricted words that require separate regulatory approval or are barred outright, and the statutory consequence of filing under a name that later turns out not to have been distinguishable. It is not the Secretary of State's official Name Reservation Request form, does not itself reserve "Meridian Ventures, Inc." or any other name with the California Secretary of State, does not constitute legal advice, and does not determine whether "Meridian Ventures, Inc." is in fact available or distinguishable. The current official form, instructions, and fee amounts are published by the California Secretary of State.]
